title: The Pot of Wisdom
originalTitle: Original Fante title not recorded in the 1917 source
sourceAuthor: William H. Barker and Cecilia Sinclair
note: A new adaptation of “How Wisdom Became the Property of the Human Race,” collected in Fante-land. Anansi is the famous spider trickster; Kweku Tsin is his son in this source.

rights.basis: Source edition published before 1929 and identified as public domain by Project Gutenberg.

artLabel: Anansi carries a clay pot toward a tall tree while his son watches.
scenes: Long ago, Father Anansi possessed all the wisdom in the world. People visited him each day to ask what to plant, how to settle arguments, and what to do when trouble came.
One day Anansi became angry with the people. “They do not deserve my wisdom,” he said.
He gathered every bit of it into a great clay pot, sealed the lid, and set off to hide it. His son, Kweku Tsin, quietly followed.
Anansi chose the tallest tree in the forest. He hung the heavy pot in front of his belly and began to climb.
The pot bumped against the trunk. It caught on every branch. Again and again, Anansi slid back to the ground.
At last Kweku Tsin called from the bushes, “Father, why not tie the pot behind you? Then it will not block your way.”
Anansi froze. He had gathered all the world’s wisdom—or so he thought—yet his son knew something that was not inside the pot.
In a flash of anger, Anansi threw the pot down. It struck a rock and shattered.
Wisdom scattered everywhere: through the forest, across the villages, and out into the wide world. That is why no one person possesses it all—and why a good idea may come from anyone.

pageArt.alt: Anansi tries to climb the tallest tree with the clay pot tied in front while his son watches below.
Wisdom scatters from the broken clay pot through the forest, village, and wide sky.
